extracted.intended_audience: early-18th-century literate English public (gentlemen and ladies) interested in manners, fashion, and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Short periodical essays and satirical how-to guidance on manners, fashion, honour, conversation, and performative social arts (e.g., use of the fan), aimed at improving or critiquing social behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive head-dress / Fontange extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not load the head with supernumerary ornaments; the head is Nature's masterpiece and adding large head-dresses destroys the symmetry of the human figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Nature 'designed the Head as the Cupola' and ornamenting it with 'childish Gewgaws, Ribbands, and Bone-lace' calls off the eye from real beauties. Historical examples: 14th-century conical head-dresses and 18th-century 'Fontanges' rose absurdly high. Anti-pattern: treating the head as a structure to be built up (women appearing like Colossi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack fashions/extravagance at opportune moments
rubrics_metrics.description: An excessive fashion is most effectively opposed when the general taste is against it — prevention is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: 'a good Reign is the only proper Time for making of Laws against the Exorbitance of Power.' Recommendation addressed to female readers as a preventative measure. Historical tactics: public denunciation and ridicule (e.g., Thomas Conecte preaching against huge head-dresses, women burning them, mobs pelting wearers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of honour: men — courage; women — chastity
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief point of honour among men is Courage, and in Women Chastity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: Each sex values most the quality that renders them amiable to the opposite sex; chivalric literature and national customs (e.g., Spanish romances) exemplify and exaggerate these ideals. Note: author contrasts this with what each sex might choose for themselves (men might value wisdom, women wit or good-nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving the lie is the greatest interpersonal affront
rubrics_metrics.description: Among violations between men, accusing another of lying is the most insulting because it implies cowardice and lack of courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural note: Saying someone 'Lies' touches the most sensible part of a man's honour and traditionally leads to blood being the only expiation. Historical/cultural example: Herodotus on Persian upbringing: truth-telling taught from youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject false notions of honour (dueling) and punish to shame
rubrics_metrics.description: The inflated, false notion of honour that leads to dueling and similar practices should be checked, shamed, and punished so as to deter it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested policy: make duellists suffer public shame (e.g., put every one that fought a Duel in the Pillory) to lower the practice's prestige. Rationale: death alone does not deter those who glory in despising it; shame and infamy are more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honour must align with religion and equity
rubrics_metrics.description: When the dictates of 'honour' are contrary to religion and equity they are a great depravity and should be exploded by government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If honour sanctions wrong ambitions or unlawful acts it becomes 'the Bane and Plague of Human Society' and must be opposed by laws and public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a disposition to be pleased — preserve good humour
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a duty to acquire and preserve a temper disposed to be pleased and to be ready for the satisfactions of life; mutual good humour seasons all social interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effects: being in a 'portable Quality of good Humour' makes every company more pleasant; even small occurrences become enjoyable. Anti-patterns: affected delicacy, constant uneasiness, and 'valetudinarians' who complain of their constitution spoil company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dominating conversation with complaints about personal ailments
rubrics_metrics.description: Recounting one's pains and aches to entertain company is the meanest help to discourse and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social rule: such narrations are poor conversational contributions; mutual good humour requires talking of matters that make friends rejoice. Example: in Sir Roger's company a complaint is met with a posset — people who keep bewailing themselves are inappropriate guests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indolence and affected delicacy; seek active taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Indolence and an affected refinement that rejects ordinary pleasures are unbecoming and reduce life below diversion; preserve vivacity, imagination, and good-breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indolence is an intermediate state between pleasure and pain; it makes life a burden. Positive traits to cultivate: lively imagination, good breeding, sweet disposition — these render one welcome and add to life's pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation should avoid shocking content and present things in their excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Good company is one where nothing is presented but in its excellence; avoid shocking or corrupting descriptions and strive to set things in the best light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: 'Beautiful Pictures are the Entertainments of pure Minds, and Deformities of the corrupted.' If speakers represent others with no ill will and set matters in best light the entertainment is delicate; otherwise conversation degrades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret old satirical/classical works with allowance for obsolete allusions
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading remote/old writings allow for obsolete words, obscure phrases, and topical allusions that aimed at then-current follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical approach: don't take literal improbable passages at face value (e.g., claims about puppet-shows, patches, languages); assume remote hints addressed particular follies in vogue that modern readers may not recognize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan exercise: commands and staged curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: A formalised regimen for the 'Exercise of the Fan' composed of commands: Handle your Fans; Unfurl your Fans; Discharge your Fans; Ground your Fans; Recover your Fans; Flutter your Fans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogy and timing: 'handle' learned in first week; 'unfurl' includes many flirts and takes about a month; 'discharge' (a loud crack) is difficult and trained to be like a pocket-pistol; 'ground' (tossing aside gracefully) may be learned in two days; 'recover' learned by practice; 'flutter' is the master-piece and can be gained in three months (teach in hot season). The entry functions both as parody and as practical stepwise instruction for learning fan gestures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan motions map to emotions and social signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Different fan motions (angry, modest, timorous, confused, merry, amorous) correspond to distinct emotional states and communicate them to observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance note: a disciplined fan reveals whether the bearer laughs, frowns, or blushes; the same fan can seem 'very angry' or 'very languishing' depending on motion. The fan may function as a social identity marker (prude or coquet). The author compiled 'The Passions of the Fan' as a mapping treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sincerity and plainness to inflated compliment and dissimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity and plain speaking are preferable to an excess of compliments and flattering dissimulation; words should correspond to the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: contemporary conversation 'swelled with Vanity and Compliment' has made words into cyphers; if words do not match thought they lose intrinsic value. Moral: to seem to be any excellence, really be it; pretence is troublesome and often exposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissimulation and artifice breed perpetual suspicion and loss of reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Artifice and dissembling bring continual inconvenience; once a man's reputation for integrity is forfeited he is not believed when he speaks truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: being caught in false pretence leads to lasting distrust — neither truth nor falsehood will serve to restore credibility. Implication for conduct: avoid dissimulation because its costs exceed apparent conveniences.
